results.title: NACCIMA, Chinese aircraft maintenance company explore investment opportunities in Nigeria's aviation sector The Nigerian Association of Cham
results.description:
NACCIMA, Chinese aircraft maintenance company explore investment opportunities in Nigeria's aviation sector

The Nigerian Association of Chambers of Commerce, Industry, Mines and Agriculture (@NACCIMA30) has explored areas of collaboration with one of China's leading aircraft maintenance companies, the Grand China Aviation Maintenance Company Limited (GCAM), with the aim of attracting foreign direct investment, accelerating industrialisation, and creating jobs for thousands of people in the country.

Led by the National President, Engr. Jani Ibrahim, mni, OON, a NACCIMA delegation visited the office of GCAM in Haikou, Hainan Province of the People's Republic of China, on Friday, November 6, 2026, for a crucial business engagement.

Also in attendance was the Consul General of Nigeria in Guangzhou, Amb. Mairo Musa Abbas, who played an important role in facilitating the meeting between NACCIMA and the aircraft maintenance company on the sidelines of the 2026 Hainan Free Trade Port International Investment Cooperation Promotion Conference.

With comprehensive capability to support a fleet of over 600 aircraft, GCAM operates as a subsidiary of HNA Technic Company Limited, which is also under the umbrella of HNA Aviation Group, the fourth largest airlines group of China.

Established in 2012, GCAM, the subsidiary company, undertakes key services such as airframe maintenance, repair, inspection, cabin renovation, overhaul, among others.

Speaking at the meeting, the National President told the management of GCAM that Nigeria will be an attractive investment destination for them. He said Nigeria boasts a huge population and is well positioned in Africa.

“It's a big opportunity for your company. We have the population you can leverage for your business. We are talking about a country of over 200 million people, with a significant air traffic. So, there is business for you in Nigeria. We invite you to come and invest here,” he said.

Engr. Ibrahim also pitched the idea of direct flight between Nigeria and China through Hainan Province, saying NACCIMA is ready for talks with the HNA Aviation Group to facilitate the arrangement. He said direct air connectivity between Nigeria and China will significantly reduce travel time, offer huge relief for travellers, and boost trade volumes between the two countries.

The NACCIMA delegation also suggested collaborations for technology transfer and training opportunities for the young population in Nigeria considering the rich experience and detailed technical strength of GCAM in the aviation sector.

The Consul General of Nigeria in Guangzhou, Amb. Abbas reaffirmed the commitment of the Consulate to initiatives that strengthen diplomatic and economic relations between Nigeria and China. She noted that both countries share a long history of cooperation, but still have a lot more area to harness for stronger economic ties and mutual benefits.

NACCIMA's strategic meeting with the management of GCAM in Hainan, China represents another milestone in its mandate of connecting businesses and opening Nigeria to sustainable global opportunities.

Signed:

Mrs Madinat Adigun-Oladotun
National Public Relations Officer
NACCIMA
November 6, 2026

results.title: PRESS STATEMENT APC'S ENDLESS LIES AND DECEIT HOW MANY TIMES WILL APC APPROVE IBOM DEEP SEA PORT?
results.description:
PRESS STATEMENT

APC'S ENDLESS LIES AND DECEIT
HOW MANY TIMES WILL APC APPROVE IBOM DEEP SEA PORT?

President Tinubu, while campaigning in Uyo, has promised and granted approval for the construction of the Ibom Deep Sea Port.

What a hocus-pocus, what hogwash, and what barefaced lies and shenanigans of a rudderless party! How many times will the APC approve the Ibom Deep Sea Port?

President Buhari approved it in December 2020. The Federal Executive Council gave approval for the implementation of the first phase of the $4.6 billion Ibom Deep Sea Port (IDSP) during its meeting on December 16, 2020.

That approval named Bollore/Power China as the preferred bidder and was meant to allow construction to commence.

In a brazen display of ignorance of statecraft and the elevation of grand deceit as a campaign strategy, President Tinubu, as APC presidential candidate, first promised the port during his 2023 campaign.

At the APC campaign rally at the Godswill Akpabio International Stadium in Uyo on 30 January 2023, he told supporters: "We will do mechanised farming. We will export food from Akwa Ibom. We will build your seaport."

Unfortunately, as is characteristic of the APC, they never fulfilled the promise. Over three years down the line, President Tinubu on Friday, 6 November 2026, had to promise again to construct the long-awaited Ibom Deep Sea Port project in Akwa Ibom State.

Obviously, this is another round of cheap promises that will not be kept or honoured. Just as before, so it will be now — empty promises. All talk and no action.

As Nigerians are still waiting for the APC and President Tinubu to give us uninterrupted electricity supply, so Akwa Ibomites are waiting endlessly for the promised deep sea port that has become a campaign tool of deceit.

Nigerians must shine their eyes and dump the APC into the abyss of socio-political irrelevance and make a new Nigeria possible.

Indeed, a New Nigeria is POssible with NDC.

Signed:
Osa Director, Esq.
For Inquiries: @DirectorOsa 
National Publicity Secretary
Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC)

results.title: A Direct Challenge to the APC and President Bola Tinubu on Nigeria’s $145 Billion Debt Profile (as at June 2026 from the DMO).
results.description:
A Direct Challenge to the APC and President Bola Tinubu on Nigeria’s $145 Billion Debt Profile (as at June 2026 from the DMO). 

Where is the Return on Investment?

According to the World Bank Group's International Debt Report 2026 released on November 6, 2026, Nigeria’s total external debt has surged to $145.02 billion. Within this astronomical portfolio, the ruling APC administration maintains a staggering $5.67 billion in bilateral debt owed to China, cementing Beijing as our largest government-to-government creditor.

As these liabilities compound, the administration continues to aggressively pursue more loans, including the latest $7.7 billion external borrowing request presented to the National Assembly to finance the budget deficit.

Debt in itself can be a tool for development, but only when it is strictly channelled into transparent, high-impact capital investments that generate economic returns. When debt rises without visible equivalents in infrastructure, it transitions from fiscal management to generational liquidation.

Therefore, the patriotic citizens of this country are asking a fundamental question: What has the APC-led administration achieved in tangible capital projects and critical investments with these billions of dollars?

To bring clarity to this national conversation and shift the focus from political rhetoric to verifiable governance, we hereby challenge the supporters of President Tinubu and the APC to step forward and name five (5) major capital projects or capital investments that have been fully initiated, completed, and officially commissioned under the presidency of Bola Ahmed Tinubu.

We do not want to hear about ongoing projects inherited from previous administrations, nor are we interested in policy declarations, macroeconomic promises, or legislative approvals. We demand an account of concrete, commissioned infrastructure that justifies the heavy debt burden being placed upon the shoulders of the Nigerian people.

True leadership is measured by the legacies it builds, not the liabilities it accumulates. Nigeria must survive, and that survival depends entirely on demanding absolute accountability from those entrusted with our national treasury.

results.title: The question for African fintech has shifted.
results.description:
The question for African fintech has shifted. In 2021, the competition was about who could raise the most. By 2026, it is about who gets to decide when you list.

OPay found out on October 30. The company priced a $304 million IPO on the NYSE and withdrew it before a single share traded, after what Bloomberg describes as an inquiry from a Chinese regulator.

What makes the case unusual is how little of OPay touches China:
- No revenue from mainland China in 2025
- Operating assets and business located outside mainland China
- Senior management mostly non Chinese citizens or not domiciled in mainland China
- Incorporated in the Cayman Islands, headquartered in Singapore
- Most revenue from Nigeria, with Indonesia, Egypt and Pakistan as the other markets

Those were the exact grounds OPay's Chinese legal advisers used in an SEC filing on October 23 to conclude no approval or filing with the China Securities Regulatory Commission was required. The same filing admitted the company could not guarantee China's overseas listing rules would never apply to it.

Seven days later, that one sentence of caution outweighed $467.1 million in half year revenue, $90.9 million in profit and 50.1 million monthly active users.

For founders raising from foreign investors, the number to watch is not the valuation. It is how many regulators can veto your exit.

OPay's $4 billion was never the problem. Its passport was.

results.title: I support the development of domestic industrial capacity.
results.description:
I support the development of domestic industrial capacity. Nigeria should not have to depend indefinitely on other countries for products it has the resources and potential to produce locally. But supporting local industry must come with conditions.

Take the petroleum market, for instance. If we are asking Nigerians to support locally refined petrol, what assurances are we giving them about price stability, supply and affordability? If the Dangote Refinery is receiving support through government policy, there must also be clear performance expectations. Can the refinery guarantee agreed supply volumes? Can it offer competitive pricing? Can it maintain consistent supply?
And if those conditions are not met, should the government not allow other qualified suppliers to compete?
That is how a healthy market should work.

I would rather see a system where the government gives indigenous industrialists the opportunity, financing support and enabling environment to build capacity, but also establishes measurable conditions for that support.

This is not an argument against Dangote. It is an argument for competition, accountability and an economic system that puts the Nigerian consumer at the centre.

Look at China. Its approach to industrial development has involved deliberate government support for domestic industries, strategic investment, technology development and the ambition to compete with established Western manufacturers.

The lesson is not that Nigeria should copy China wholesale. It is that countries that take industrial development seriously do not simply wait for their industries to become competitive. They create policies and institutions that help them get there.

That is what economic leadership should look like: not simply reacting to developments, but anticipating them and positioning the country to benefit.
